**Question #1:** 
Set up a vector named age, consisting of 15, 28, 32, 36, 27, 18, 52, 39, 42, 29, 35, 31, 27, 22, 37, 34, 19, 20, 57, 49, 50, 37, 46, 25, 17, 12, 42, 53, 41, 51, 35, 24, 33, 8.

```{r}
age <- c(15, 28, 32, 36, 27, 18, 52, 39, 42, 29, 35, 31, 27, 22, 37, 34, 19, 20, 57, 49, 50, 37, 46, 25, 17, 12, 42, 53, 41, 51, 35, 24, 33, 8)
```

a. How many data points?
- The vector named "age" has 34 data points. 

b. Find the reciprocal of age?

```{r}
age <- c(15, 28, 32, 36, 27, 18, 52, 39, 42, 29, 35, 31, 27, 22, 37, 34, 19, 20, 57, 49, 50, 37, 46, 25, 17, 12, 42, 53, 41, 51, 35, 24, 33, 8)

reciprocal_age <- 1/age
reciprocal_age
```
 
c. Assign also new_age <- c(age, 0, age). What happens to new_age?

```{r}
age <- c(15, 28, 32, 36, 27, 18, 52, 39, 42, 29, 35, 31, 27, 22, 37, 34, 19, 20, 57, 49, 50, 37, 46, 25, 17, 12, 42, 53, 41, 51, 35, 24, 33, 8)

new_age <- c(age, 0, age)
new_age
```
- The vector "age" is copied and the the "0" is put at the middle and again the vector "age is copied, so it means that the vector "age is doubled in the vector "new_age" and the "0" is added in the middle of them. 

d. Find the minimum and the maximum value of age.

```{r}
age <- c(15, 28, 32, 36, 27, 18, 52, 39, 42, 29, 35, 31, 27, 22, 37, 34, 19, 20, 57, 49, 50, 37, 46, 25, 17, 12, 42, 53, 41, 51, 35, 24, 33, 8)

new_age <- c(age, 0, age)
min(new_age)
max(new_age)
```

**Question #2:** 
rep(c("A","B"), each = 2) and rep(c("A","B"), times = 2) both produce a vector of length 4, but with different element orders.
Explain in your own words the
difference between each and times.

-rep(c("A","B"), each = 2) and rep(c("A","B"), times = 2) both produce a vector length of 4 but have different elements order because 
rep(c("A","B"), each = 2) repeat each vector 2 times, while rep(c("A","B"), times = 2) repeat a vector 2 times.

**Question #3:**
Compare seq(1, 20, by = 2) with seq(1, 20, length.out = 5). What does each argument (by vs length.out) control, and when would you use one over the other in a real analysis?

-So seq(1, 20, by = 2) is used to set the steps between the numbers and is used to have a fixed intervals between 2 units. While seq(1, 20, length.out = 5) creates exactly that many evenly spaced values and is used to know how many points you need. So "by" is use for fixed steps and the "length.out" is used when you need a specific number of points across a range.

grades[c(1,4)]

grades[c("Science", "PE")]

```

# negative indexing, e.g. grades[-c(...)]

grades[-c(1,4)]

```

```{r}

names(grades) <- c("Math", "Science", "English", "History", "PE")

grades[grades >= 85]

```


**Question #5:** 
 -Negative indexing (grades[-1]) removes an element, while logical indexing (grades[grades >= 85]) filters by a condition.

 -Describe a real situation where you would need negative indexing, and a different situation where logical indexing would be the better tool.
 
-Negative indexing it use when you know exactly which position to remove like dropping one outlier row you already identified. While logical indexing is used when you want to keep everything that's meets a rule, for example keeping only test scores above a passing threshold.

**Question #6:**
```{r}
# -What happens if you run grades[10] (an index that doesn’t exist)? Run it, observe the result, and explain why R responds this way instead of throwing an error.

grades <- c(85, 90, 78, 92, 88, 76)
grades[10]

```
-Running grades[10] return NA instead of an error because in R, it treats the missing position as "unknown value" rather than crashing your whole script. This way, code keeps running even when some indices don't exist.

**Question #8:**
```{r}
 #-In the vectors-recycling chunk, z has 6 elements and short has only 2. R still produced an answer instead of an error.

 #-Explain, in your own words, what R’s “recycling rule” did to short to make the addition work.

z <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
short <- c(1, 0)

z + short
```

-R uses its recycling rule to repeat a shorter vector when performing element-wise operations. If the longer vector's length is a multiple of the shorter vector's length, recycling generally occurs without a warning. Otherwise, R warns that the lengths are not exact multiples. 

**Question #9:**

```{r}
#Now try adding z (length 6) to c(1, 0, 1) (length 3) instead. Does it work cleanly?
z <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)

z + c(1, 0, 1)

```

```{r}
#Then try adding z to c(1, 0, 1, 1) (length 4). Compare the warning (or lack of one) in each case, and explain what condition determines whether R recycles silently versus with a warning.

z <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)

z + c(1, 0, 1, 1)
```
-R recycles without a warning when the longer vectors length is a multiple of the shorter vectors length.Otherwise, it gives a warning because the recycling is incomplete.

## Part D — Lists: Creating and Subsetting

```{r}
# TODO: Create a list called student with these named elements:
# name = "Maria Santos", age = 20, grades = c(88, 92, 79),
# is_enrolled = TRUE

student <- list(
  name = "Maria Santos",
  age = 20,
  grades = c(88, 92, 79),
  is_enrolled = TRUE
)

# TODO: Access the "grades" element of student using single brackets
# student["grades"] -- then check its type with class()

student["grades"]
class(student["grades"])

# TODO: Access the "grades" element of student using double brackets
# student[["grades"]] -- then check its type with class()

student["grades"]
class(student[["grades"]])

# TODO: Access the "name" element of student using the $ operator
# student$name

student$name

# TODO: From student, extract just the SECOND grade in the grades vector
# in a single expression, e.g. student[["grades"]][2] or student$grades[2]

student[["grades"]][2]

```

**Question #10:**

 -student["grades"] and student[["grades"]] look similar but return objects of different classes.

 -Run class() on each and explain the difference in what single-bracket [ ] versus double-bracket [[ ]] return from a list.
 
```{r}
student <- list(
  name = "Maria Santos",
  age = 20,
  grades = c(88, 92, 79),
  is_enrolled = TRUE
)

class(student["grades"])

class(student[["grades"]])
```

-The single brackets[] return a list containing the selected element.
-The double brackets[[]] extract the element itself. 


**Question #11:**

Why do you think R makes a distinction between [ ] and [[ ]] for lists, but a vector only needs [ ]? Think about what a list can contain that a vector cannot.

-List can contain different data types, so R provides both ways to select elements.A vector generally contains values of the same type and uses [] for subsetting. 

## Part E — Critical Thinking Challenge

```{r}
inventory <- list(
  item = c("Notebook", "Pen", "Eraser"),
  price = c(25.50, 10.00, 5.00),
  in_stock = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

# TODO: Using what you learned in Parts B and D, print only the items
# (from inventory$item) that are currently in stock (in_stock == TRUE)

inventory$item[inventory$in_stock]
```

```{r}
# TODO: A new product "Ruler" priced at 15.00 and in stock (TRUE) needs
# to be added to inventory. Use append() to add "Ruler" to
# inventory$item, 15.00 to inventory$price, and TRUE to inventory$in_stock.
# (You will need three separate append() calls, one per vector.)

inventory$item <- append(inventory$item, "Ruler")

inventory$price <- append(inventory$price, 15.00)

inventory$in_stock <- append(inventory$in_stock, TRUE)

inventory
```
